## The question

Spain has one of the highest early school leaving rates in Europe. The aggregate
figure is well known; what is far less clear is *which students* are at risk,
and on what evidence a guidance counsellor could act before a student drops out
rather than after.

This project had a specific audience from the start: vocational-training
guidance counsellors, who are not statisticians and who need something they can
open, explore and use in a meeting.

## The data

Three sources, deliberately combined:

- **PISA 2022** student questionnaires — the international assessment run by the
  OECD. The source file is a 2 GB SPSS export, which drives most of the
  preprocessing work.
- **ELET indicator** by autonomous community, to place each Spanish region
  against the European benchmark.
- **Spanish Ministry of Education** figures on vocational-training dropout.

The target variable, `en_riesgo`, was constructed from student performance
across the three PISA competences, rather than taken off the shelf. That
definition is a modelling decision, not a given, and it is the one I would
challenge first if someone disagreed with the results.

## The method

Context variables in PISA are overwhelmingly categorical — family situation,
school resources, attitudes — which rules out the usual correlation-first
approach. **Multiple Correspondence Analysis** was used to reduce that
categorical space and reveal natural groupings of students.

Two models were then trained side by side, for different reasons. **Logistic
regression** gives a counsellor something explainable: coefficients that can be
defended in a conversation with a family. **Random Forest** gives better
detection. Both were judged on recall in the risk class rather than on overall
accuracy, because in this problem a missed at-risk student costs far more than
a false alarm.

## What came out

| Model | Overall accuracy | Recall, risk class |
|---|---|---|
| Logistic regression | — | 60% |
| Random Forest | 81% | 64% |

The gap between 81% accuracy and 64% recall is the honest headline here: the
model is considerably better at confirming that a student is fine than at
catching one who is not. For a screening tool that is the wrong way round, and
it is the first thing I would work on with more data.

MCA surfaced coherent student profiles that map onto the risk classification,
which matters more than the model scores for the intended use: counsellors
recognise the profiles, and recognising them is what turns a number into a
conversation.

The whole analysis was delivered as an interactive Tableau story rather than a
report, so the audience can filter to their own region and cohort instead of
reading about someone else's.

## Stack

Python · Pandas · NumPy · Scikit-learn · prince (MCA) · Matplotlib · Seaborn ·
Tableau
